title: Structured Logging
description: Learn structured logging with Serilog and semantic formats.

data.text: **Structured logging** stores log events as discrete key-value properties (typically serialized as JSON) instead of an opaque string. This makes the data **queryable**, **aggregatable**, and **searchable** in tools like Seq, Elasticsearch, Splunk, Application Insights, or Datadog.

data.title: Why structured logging?
data.text: Plain-text logs are great for humans but terrible for machines. Structured logs let you ask real questions: "how many 500-errors did tenant 42 see in the last hour?" — without writing regex.

data.caption: How a structured log event flows from code to sink

Console, File, Seq] D --> E[(JSON / columnar store)]

data.text: **Serilog** is a popular structured logging library for .NET. Its message-template syntax (`{PropertyName}`) preserves the value as a first-class property rather than concatenating it into a string.

data.title: Structured log message with Serilog
data.content: Use named placeholders so the value is captured as a property, not just text.

terms.definition: A string with `{Name}` placeholders that Serilog preserves as structured properties.
Adds extra properties (MachineName, RequestId, TenantId) to every log event.
Where log events are written — Console, File, Seq, Elasticsearch, etc.
Serilog formatter that emits one JSON object per line (CLEF format), ideal for log aggregators.

data.title: Don't log secrets
data.text: Even with structured logging, you can accidentally serialize a `Password` or `ConnectionString` property. Use `[NotLogged]` attributes, custom destructuring policies, or simply exclude sensitive fields.

data.title: Logging exceptions with structured context
data.content: Capture the exception as a property and add ambient context with LogContext.

data.title: Switch to structured logging
data.description: Replace the default ASP.NET Core logger with Serilog and verify the JSON output.
steps: In Program.cs, replace `builder.Logging` with `builder.Host.UseSerilog()` and configure a Console sink that uses `RenderedCompactJsonFormatter`.
In an existing controller, change one `_logger.LogInformation("...")` call to use a `{UserId}` placeholder.
Run the API and verify the console now emits one JSON object per line.
Pipe the JSON into `jq` or another tool and query by the new property.
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to filter console output by a structured field (e.g. only logs where UserId = 42) without regex.

items.text: Push ambient context with `LogContext.PushProperty` for request/tenant/correlation IDs.
Use `@` for object destructuring when you want its properties captured.
Write JSON to stdout so log shippers can ingest it cleanly.
Mask or exclude secrets and PII before the log hits a sink.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Structured logs use named properties, not concatenated strings.
Serilog's message-template syntax preserves properties end-to-end.
JSON output (e.g. CompactJsonFormatter) is the lingua franca of log aggregators.
Enrichers add ambient context (machine, request, tenant) automatically.
Tools like Seq, Elasticsearch and Application Insights make structured logs truly queryable.
data.takeaway: Structured logging turns logs from strings into searchable, aggregatable events.
